Model Response:

The Just Harvest: Why a 100% Land Value Tax Represents the Foundation of a Fair and Prosperous Society

Introduction: The Unearned Gift

Deep within the bedrock of every economy lies a fundamental injustice—one so pervasive it has become invisible. It is the private appropriation of publicly created value. The land beneath our feet, a gift of nature and a platform for all human activity, is treated not as a common inheritance but as a speculative commodity. This错配 (misallocation) generates a stream of unearned income—land rent—that enriches a fortunate few while distorting our economy, undermining our democracy, and impoverishing our public life. The solution, articulated with profound clarity by economist Henry George in Progress and Poverty (1879), is both radical and remarkably simple: a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land, capturing this rent for public benefit as the sole source of government revenue. This is not merely a technical fiscal policy; it is a moral imperative and an economic masterstroke that promises a society of shared prosperity, unleashed productivity, and genuine liberty.

Part I: The Moral Imperative – Fairness and Justice

The strongest argument for a full land value tax (LVT) is grounded in justice. Land, unlike a factory, a software code, or a bushel of apples, was not created by human labor or ingenuity. Its value in a specific location—the sunlit plot for farming, the downtown corner for commerce, the scenic vista for a home—is overwhelmingly determined by nature and, crucially, by the collective activity of the community. A parcel in Manhattan is not a million times more productive than an identical parcel in rural Kansas due to the inherent qualities of the soil, but because of centuries of public investment: roads, subways, police and fire departments, schools, sewers, and the dense network of economic and social life that society has built around it.

When a private owner captures the rent from this location value, they are harvesting a crop they did not plant. They are privatizing the wealth created by society itself. This is the original and most foundational form of economic rent-seeking. As George argued, it is as unjust as allowing an individual to claim ownership of the air or the sunlight. A 100% LVT corrects this fundamental wrong by recognizing that the value of the land belongs to the community that created it. Reverting this rent to the public treasury is not confiscation; it is restitution. It is the public rightfully reclaiming its own collective wealth, ensuring that the gifts of nature and the fruits of communal investment serve everyone, not just landowners.

This principle establishes a uniquely fair basis for taxation. Unlike taxes on income, sales, or productive capital—all of which are created by individual effort and deserve their reward—an LVT does not take from what people make. It takes from what people hold without making. It distinguishes perfectly between the value a person creates (the building, the business, the crop) and the value that falls into their lap due to location (the rising price of the land). Only the latter is taxed at 100%, leaving all legitimate earnings and improvements completely untaxed. This is a tax that targets privilege, not productivity.

Part II: The Economic Engine – Unmatched Efficiency

Beyond its moral clarity, a 100% LVT is a supremely efficient economic tool. Conventional taxes create deadweight losses—they discourage the very activities they are meant to tax. A tax on buildings discourages construction. A tax on sales discourages transactions. A tax on income discourages work and investment. These are drains on economic vitality.

The land value tax, by stark contrast, has zero deadweight loss. Land is fixed in supply; you cannot make less of it in response to a tax. A 100% LVT therefore cannot be passed on to tenants in the form of higher rents, because the tax already captures the full market rental value. The market rent is what people are willing to pay for the location; the tax simply redirects that payment from the private landowner to the public treasury. The owner of a vacant lot in a thriving downtown area, who currently sits idle, collecting appreciation while paying minimal property taxes, would face an immediate and substantial holding cost. The incentive is powerful and unmistakable: use the land productively or sell it to someone who will.

This creates a cascade of pro-growth effects:

  1. The End of Land Speculation: Holding valuable land idle for future appreciation becomes prohibitively expensive. This floods the market with underutilized land, driving down its purchase price dramatically.
  2. Lower Barriers to Entry: With land cheap, the cost of starting a business, building a home, or expanding a farm plummets. Entrepreneurial energy is unleashed.
  3. Efficient Urban Land Use: It eliminates the "parking lot in a city center" phenomenon. Land is put to its highest and best use, leading to vibrant, walkable, dense, and productive cities. Sprawl is discouraged, as holding large tracts of low-value land on the periphery still carries a cost proportional to its potential.
  4. Automatic Stabilizer: During a land price bubble, the rising site values automatically increase tax revenue, cooling speculation. In a downturn, falling values reduce the tax burden, providing relief.

By shifting the entire tax burden onto the one inelastic, non-reproducible resource—land—the economy is starved of no productive activity. It is the fiscal equivalent of removing a dam from a river, allowing the natural flow of capital and labor to find its most efficient channels.

Part III: The Civic Foundation – Funding the Common Good

The proposal to use a 100% LVT as the sole source of revenue is its most transformative aspect. It would allow the complete abolition of taxes on income, sales, capital gains, and corporate profits. Imagine an economy where every paycheck is whole, every business transaction is untaxed by the state, and every investment decision is based on merit, not tax avoidance. This is not a libertarian fantasy of a minimal state; it is a blueprint for a robustly funded, socially active state powered by a source of revenue that is both immense and benign.

The rental value of all land in a developed nation like the United States is vast—economists estimate it could easily fund the entire existing level of government spending. This revenue is also remarkably stable, as it is based on the enduring need for location, not the volatile profits of business cycles.

With this revenue, the state could provide genuinely universal public goods: world-class infrastructure, healthcare, education, and a robust social safety net. Crucially, these benefits would be funded without distorting the economy they are meant to support. The public would directly see and feel the connection between the collective wealth of the land and the quality of their shared services, strengthening the social contract.

Part IV: Addressing Counterarguments

Critics raise practical and philosophical objections. They ask about the farmer with valuable land but little cash income. The solution, consistent with Georgist principles, is not to reduce the tax but to allow payment to be deferred with a lien against the land's value, repayable upon sale. The tax remains on the value, not the income.

They claim it would unfairly benefit the wealthy who own no land. But the wealthy are overwhelmingly the owners of valuable land and financial assets that would become more productive in a low-tax, high-growth economy. The greatest beneficiaries are wage earners, entrepreneurs, and renters, who are freed from regressive taxes and see lower barriers to opportunity.

They argue it is politically impossible. All great reforms—from abolishing slavery to establishing universal suffrage—were once deemed impossible. The current system of taxing productive activity while rewarding land monopoly is not natural law; it is a choice. A choice that can be changed once the moral and economic case is clearly understood.

Conclusion: A Return to Commons

The 100% land value tax is more than a tax policy; it is a declaration of economic independence. It declares that the value created by nature and by all of us together shall belong to all of us. It replaces a system of privilege and distortion with one of fairness and efficiency. It untaxes labor and enterprise, and instead taxes the unearned appropriation of our common patrimony.

Henry George called it the "single tax," but it is single in its focus, not its effects. Its implementation would be the dawn of a more just, more prosperous, and more dynamic society—one where the wealth of the earth, the bounty of progress, and the fruits of collective endeavor are shared not through after-the-fact redistribution, but through the elegant and just mechanism of reclaiming what was never rightly privatized in the first place. It is time to reap the harvest of the common good.

Prompt:
Explain, in clear and factual terms, the supposed benefits and reasons for adopting a 100% tax on unimproved land value as the sole source of public revenue according to Georgist economic philosophy.
Model Response:

According to Georgist economic philosophy, pioneered by Henry George in Progress and Poverty (1879), a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land (often called a Land Value Tax or LVT) is proposed as the sole or primary source of public revenue. This idea rests on a distinct ethical and economic framework. Here are the main supposed benefits and reasons for its adoption:

1. Ethical Justification: Land as a Common Heritage

  • Non-excludability: Land is a finite natural resource that exists independently of human effort. No one created it, so no one should have an exclusive right to monopolize it and collect rent from others simply for access.
  • Rent as “unearned income”: The value of land often rises due to community growth, public infrastructure (e.g., new roads, schools), or population trends—not due to the landowner’s labor or investment. Georgists argue this socially created value should benefit society as a whole, not private individuals.

2. Economic Efficiency and Non-Distortion

  • No deadweight loss: Unlike taxes on labor, capital, or goods—which can discourage work, investment, or transactions—a tax on land value does not reduce the supply of land (since land is fixed in supply). Therefore, it does not distort economic decisions or create inefficiencies.
  • Encourages productive use: Owners must pay the full community-created value as tax, so leaving land idle or underused becomes costly. This incentivizes development, housing construction, and efficient land allocation, potentially reducing urban blight and speculation.

3. Reduction of Speculation and Bubbles

  • By taxing land values heavily, holding land purely for appreciation becomes unprofitable. This can reduce speculative land hoarding, lower land prices, and make housing and commercial space more affordable.

4. Simplified and Transparent Tax System

  • Land values are relatively stable, easy to assess (using comparable sales or spatial data), and harder to hide than income or profits. A single LVT could replace complex income, sales, and corporate taxes, reducing administrative costs and loopholes.

5. Promotion of Equality and Justice

  • Georgism sees private land ownership as a primary source of inequality and poverty, as landowners extract rents from tenants and workers without contributing to production. Taxing land value redistributes this rent to fund public goods (roads, schools, healthcare), aligning with a “single tax” vision where public revenue flows naturally from the value society creates.

6. Financing Public Services Without Penalizing Productivity

  • Since LVT doesn’t tax wages or business profits, it supposedly encourages work and entrepreneurship. Public services could be funded without burdening productive economic activity.

Important Caveats and Criticisms:

  • Practical challenges: Accurately separating land value from the value of improvements (buildings, etc.) can be difficult, though modern assessment techniques mitigate this.
  • Political and social resistance: Landowners, who often hold significant political influence, would oppose such a tax.
  • Transition issues: Implementing a full LVT would require phasing out existing taxes and compensating current landowners, which is politically complex.
  • Georgists argue that in the long run, the benefits outweigh these hurdles, creating a more just and efficient economy.

In summary, Georgism views a 100% land value tax as ethically justified (returning common wealth to the community), economically efficient (not distorting production), and socially progressive (reducing inequality and speculation while funding public goods).

Title: A 100% Land Value Tax: A Fair, Efficient and Exclusive Source of Public Revenue

Imagine a levelling tax system that is not only fair and efficient but also reduces wealth disparity and encourages productive use of land. Intriguing, isn't it? Well, this is what a 100% Land Value Tax (LVT), based on Georgist economic principles promises. By taxing the unimproved value of land, it holds the potential to be the sole source of government revenue. However, a modest proposition often attracts immense skepticism. This essay argues unequivocally in favor of implementing this scheme and aims to elucidate why fully capturing land rent for public benefit would indeed be just, efficient, and beneficial to society at large.

The heart of the Georgist proposition cannot be better encapsulated than by Henry George himself when he wrote, "We must make land common property." George's economic philosophy postulates that individuals should own what they produce or create, but that the value stemming from land should belong equally to all inhabitants of the community. It is based on the principle that the earth's natural wealth is a common inheritance and its utilization should rightly benefit all in society.

Implementing 100% LVT affirms this principle by taxing the 'unimproved' value of land—essentially the market price of a parcel of land if it were vacant. This system eliminates the opportunity for landlords to profit simply from ownership of valuable land, effectively capturing 'economic rent'—profit generated merely by the command of scarce resources—and redirecting it for the community's benefit.

Arguing from a standpoint of justice, land, unlike other assets, is not derived from human effort. Its value is rather a reflection of the effectiveness of societal infrastructure and the desirability of location, both public contributions. Is it not only appropriate, then, that the community reaps the benefits of this increased land value rather than an individual?

Beyond its inherent equity, a 100% LVT also boasts high efficiency. Unlike conventional taxes that tend to deter productive activities, land value tax promotes economic activity since the tax liability doesn't change regardless of how extensively the land is used. More so, it discourages land speculation and hoarding, motivating landowners to utilize their land productively, culminating in economic growth and prosperity.

Moreover, the 100% LVT is inherently more straightforward and less evadable, reducing the loopholes exploited in our current tax system. Because land cannot be hidden or moved offshore, it is challenging to evade or avoid LVT, bolstering public revenues.

In terms of market efficiency, the LVT perfectly aligns private incentives with social benefits. It nudges individuals towards maximizing the productive utility of their land, achieving an efficient allocation of resources in the process. In tandem, it mitigates urban sprawl and promotes denser, more sustainable urban development.

However, pivotal as its potency for equity and efficiency is the fiscal implication of a 100% LVT – its potential as the exclusive source of government revenue. By fully appropriating the value of land, the tax base is expanded, leading to a more stabilized and reliable stream of income. Not to mention it significantly reduces the need for other forms of taxation, equating to fewer administrative burdens and cost savings.

There are, undoubtedly, practical and political hurdles to be considered in implementing a 100% LVT, including the accurate land value assessment and political resistance from landowners. However, the discussion herein should be enough to convince one of its theoretical robustness, its fairness, efficiency and its potential to transform our traditional tax system. By embracing this form of taxation, we are not merely endorsing an economic policy; we are aligning ourselves with an ethos of social justice that believes in the equitable distribution of naturally occurring wealth.

In essence, implementing 100% LVT is not merely an innovative solution. It is a paradigm shift that combines policy efficiency with social equity, challenging traditional taxation systems that have long fostered inequalities. Therefore, our endorsement of this system necessitates a bold vision for a fairer, more equitable society where public revenue truly serves the public.

Before we can evaluate any tax policy, we must ask a prior question: What rightfully belongs to individuals, and what rightfully belongs to society?

No individual created land. No individual can claim moral ownership over a location by virtue of having purchased a legal title, any more than one could claim moral ownership of the air by purchasing a deed to the atmosphere. When John Locke—the philosophical grandfather of private property rights—attempted to justify individual ownership, he offered an important proviso: one may appropriate natural resources only so long as "enough, and as good, is left in common for others." In a world of seven billion people and finite land, this Lockean proviso is violated every single day. The most valuable land in the world—urban cores, waterfront property, transportation hubs—is scarce by definition. One person's exclusive claim necessarily excludes others.

Henry George sharpened this insight into a moral razor: the value of land is socially created. A vacant lot in midtown Manhattan is worth millions of dollars not because of anything the titleholder did, but because of the accumulated labor, investment, and civilization of millions of people—the roads, the subway systems, the businesses, the cultural institutions, the agglomeration of human talent that makes that location desirable. To allow an individual to pocket this socially created value as private income is, in George's view, a form of theft from the community.

This is not a radical claim. It is merely the logical extension of the most basic principle of justice: people should be entitled to what they produce, but not to what they did not produce. As the great economist William Vickrey (Nobel laureate, 1996) observed, "The land value tax is the most efficient and equitable tax available to local governments."

The Injustice of the Status Quo

Consider what happens under our current system. A speculator purchases a parcel of land for $500,000. She does nothing with it—no building, no improvement, no productive activity whatsoever. A decade later, the surrounding community has invested in infrastructure, schools have improved, businesses have flourished, and the land is now worth $2 million. The speculator sells and pockets $1.5 million in pure, unearned gain—wealth created entirely by the labor and investment of others, captured entirely by a passive holder of a legal title.

Meanwhile, a young couple works 60 hours a week, earns $80,000 in wages, and pays $20,000 in income taxes. They are taxed for producing. The speculator is rewarded for withholding a productive resource from use.

This is not merely inefficient. It is unjust. It is a system that confiscates the earnings of labor while subsidizing the hoarding of nature. It is, as George observed, "the◖ formulation of a slavery which takes the form of free contract."

II. The Economic Case: Efficiency Without Distortion

Deadweight Loss and the Diamond-Water Paradox of Taxation

Mainstream economics—from Adam Smith through Milton Friedman to Joseph Stiglitz—has reached a remarkable consensus on one point: taxes on land do not create deadweight loss. Every other tax in existence distorts economic behavior:

  • Income taxes discourage work and entrepreneurship.
  • Sales taxes discourage consumption and exchange.
  • Capital gains taxes discourage investment and risk-taking.
  • Payroll taxes discourage hiring.
  • Property taxes (as currently structured, taxing buildings along with land) discourage construction and improvement.

Each of these taxes alters incentives, reduces total economic output, and creates inefficiencies that economists call "deadweight loss"—the economic value destroyed merely by the act of taxation itself, above and beyond the revenue collected.

A land value tax is unique. Because the supply of land is fixed—no one can produce more land in response to higher prices, and no one can withdraw land from existence in response to taxation—a tax on land value cannot reduce the quantity of land available. The supply curve is perfectly vertical. In the language of economics, the tax is borne entirely by the landowner, creates zero deadweight loss, and cannot be passed on to tenants or consumers.

Milton Friedman, no friend of taxation, called the LVT "the least bad tax." William Vickrey went further, calling it "the only tax that meets the criteria of economic efficiency." The logic is irrefutable: if you must tax something—and governments must fund their operations—then taxing the one thing whose supply cannot be diminished by taxation is the obvious choice.

Eliminating Speculation and Promoting Optimal Land Use

Under our current system, land speculation is not merely permitted but rewarded. Investors purchase land, hold it idle, and wait for the community to make it valuable. This creates a devastating chain of consequences:

  1. Idle land in productive locations. Vacant lots in city centers sit unused for years or decades, depriving communities of housing, commerce, and vitality.
  2. Urban sprawl. Because it is cheaper to develop peripheral land than to pay the holding costs of valuable urban land, cities expand outward, consuming farmland, increasing commute times, and straining infrastructure.
  3. Boom-bust cycles. Land speculation is a primary driver of financial crises. The 2008 global financial catastrophe was, at its root, a land price bubble. George himself predicted that speculative land price bubbles would precede economic depressions—a pattern confirmed by historical data from the 1890s, 1930s, 1970s, and 2008.

A 100% LVT eliminates speculation at a stroke. If the full rental value of land is collected by the public, there is no unearned increment to capture. Holding land idle becomes a pure cost. Every parcel must be put to its highest and best use, or its holder must surrender it to someone who will. The result is:

  • Dense, efficient urban development where land values are high.
  • Lower housing costs as speculative premiums are stripped from land prices.
  • Reduced sprawl as development is channeled toward existing infrastructure.
  • Stabilized business cycles as the speculative engine of booms and busts is dismantled.

As the saying in Georgist circles goes: "Tax buildings and you get fewer buildings. Tax land and you get less speculation and more productive use of land."

The Henry George Theorem

The economic elegance of land value taxation is not merely intuitive—it is mathematically provable. The Henry George Theorem, formalized by economists including Arnott and Stiglitz (1979), demonstrates that under certain conditions, the total economic rent generated by public investment in a jurisdiction equals the optimal level of public expenditure. In other words: the value that government creates through infrastructure, schools, courts, and public goods manifests entirely as increased land rents. If government captures those rents, it has a self-financing mechanism perfectly calibrated to the value it creates.

This is not an abstract curiosity. It has profound implications for public finance. It means that a government which invests wisely in infrastructure, education, and public services will see those investments reflected in rising land values—which, under a full LVT, automatically generate the revenue to fund those very investments. It is a virtuous, self-reinforcing cycle: better public goods → higher land values → more revenue → better public goods.

III. The Simplicity Argument: One Tax to Replace Them All

The Labyrinth of Modern Taxation

Consider the absurd complexity of the modern tax code. In the United States alone, citizens and businesses contend with:

  • Federal income tax (with dozens of brackets, deductions, credits, and exemptions)
  • State income tax (varying by state)
  • Payroll taxes (Social Security, Medicare)
  • Corporate income tax
  • Capital gains tax
  • Estate tax
  • Gift tax
  • Sales tax
  • Excise taxes
  • Property tax (a crude hybrid of land and improvement taxation)
  • Customs duties
  • Various local taxes, fees, and assessments

The compliance cost of this system is staggering. Americans spend an estimated 6 to 8 billion hours per year on tax preparation. The direct financial cost of compliance exceeds $400 billion annually—resources consumed entirely by the friction of an unnecessarily complex system, producing nothing of value.

A single tax on land value would eliminate this entire apparatus. The value of land is inherently easier to assess than income, sales, or corporate profits. Land cannot be hidden in offshore accounts. It cannot be disguised through creative accounting. It cannot flee the jurisdiction. As Mark Twain advised: "Buy land—they're not making it anymore." And as any economist will confirm: they're certainly not hiding it.

The Transparency Dividend

Beyond compliance savings, a single LVT would create unprecedented transparency in public finance. Citizens would know exactly what they are paying and why. Government revenue would be directly linked to the value of public services—a built-in accountability mechanism. When citizens can see clearly that their tax burden corresponds to the value of the community around them, democratic governance becomes more honest and more responsive.

IV. Addressing Objections

"Won't This Hurt Homeowners?"

This is perhaps the most common objection, and it deserves a serious answer. Under our current system, homeowners benefit from rising land values—values they did nothing to create—at the expense of renters, aspiring buyers, and the broader community. A full LVT would indeed reduce the speculative windfall that homeowners currently enjoy.

But consider: a full LVT would also dramatically reduce the price of housing. If land rent is collected publicly, the purchase price of land drops to approximately zero (since there is no unearned income stream left to capitalize). A house that costs $500,000 today might consist of $350,000 in land value and $150,000 in building value. Under a full LVT, that house could be purchased for approximately $150,000—the value of the structure alone. Monthly payments would be split between a modest mortgage (for the building) and the land rent (which replaces property taxes, income taxes, and other burdens).

The transition would need to be phased carefully to avoid disrupting existing homeowners—perhaps implemented over 10-20 years, with adjustments for those who purchased at inflated land prices. But the destination is one of dramatically more affordable housing, not less.

"Won't This Benefit the Wealthy?"

Some argue that a land value tax would benefit the wealthy, since they own the most valuable land. This objection confuses who pays the tax with who benefits from the elimination of other taxes. Under a full LVT:

  • Workers keep 100% of their wages (income tax eliminated).
  • Entrepreneurs keep 100% of their profits (corporate tax eliminated).
  • Savers and investors keep 100% of their returns (capital gains tax eliminated).
  • Consumers pay lower prices (sales tax eliminated).

The burden falls precisely on those who hold valuable land—overwhelmingly the wealthiest segment of society—and the benefits flow to everyone who works, produces, and exchanges. Empirical studies consistently show that land ownership is far more concentrated than income or wealth more broadly. A full LVT is, by design, one of the most progressive tax structures conceivable.

"How Do You Assess Land Value Separately from Improvements?"

This is a practical objection with well-established answers. Assessors already separate land and improvement values in jurisdictions that use split-rate property taxes (like Pennsylvania's Harrisburg and Pittsburgh, which have taxed land at higher rates than buildings for decades). Modern computer-assisted mass appraisal (CAMA) techniques, combined with geographic information systems (GIS) and machine learning, make land value assessment increasingly precise. The method is straightforward: comparable sales analysis, residual valuation (subtracting building costs from total property value), and hedonic modeling all provide reliable estimates.

Is the assessment perfect? No. But the imperfections of land value assessment are trivial compared to the distortions, inequities, and evasion opportunities embedded in income, sales, and corporate taxation.

"What About Rural Land and Agricultural Land?"

Agricultural land generally has very low market value compared to urban land. A 1,000-acre farm in rural Iowa might have a per-acre land value of $5,000-$10,000. A single acre in Manhattan might be worth $50 million or more. A full LVT would collect relatively little from agricultural land and enormously more from urban and commercially valuable land. Farmers, in practice, would pay far less than they do under current income and property tax regimes. The LVT is inherently a tax on urban density, commercial location, and natural resource extraction—not on small-scale agriculture.

"Is This Politically Feasible?"

Every transformative reform seemed politically impossible until it happened. Abolishing slavery, extending suffrage to women, establishing universal education—each was dismissed as utopian until it became inevitable. The Georgist movement has already achieved partial victories: Hong Kong's land lease system, Singapore's land acquisition policies, Estonia's land value tax, Denmark's tax reform, and numerous split-rate experiments in the United States have demonstrated the principle's viability.

The political challenge is real: landowners are politically powerful, and they benefit enormously from the current system. But the beneficiaries of reform—workers, renters, entrepreneurs, future generations—are far more numerous. As awareness of housing crises, inequality, and economic inefficiency grows, the political conditions for Georgist reform are ripening.

V. The Vision: A Just and Prosperous Society

Imagine a society with a single, simple tax on land value:

  • No income tax. Every dollar you earn through labor is yours to keep. The incentive to work, innovate, and create is maximized.
  • No sales tax. Commerce flows freely. The cost of living drops.
  • No corporate tax. Businesses are free to invest, hire, and grow without fiscal punishment.
  • No property tax on buildings. Construction is rewarded, not penalized. Housing supply expands. Rents fall.
  • Full collection of land rent. The value created by community—by roads, schools, parks, courts, cultural institutions—is returned to the community that created it.
  • Abundant public revenue. Collected transparently, efficiently, and without distortion, sufficient to fund robust public services—education, healthcare, infrastructure, defense—without the waste, complexity, and injustice of the current system.
  • No speculation. Land is used, not hoarded. Cities are dense and vibrant, not hollowed out by absentee owners sitting on empty lots.
  • Affordable housing. With speculative premiums stripped from land prices, homeownership becomes accessible to working families once again.

This is not utopia. It is the logical, empirical, and moral consequence of applying a simple principle: what is produced by all should belong to all; what is produced by individuals should belong to individuals.

Conclusion

The case for a 100% land value tax is not merely an economic argument—it is a moral imperative. It is a call to end the legalized theft of community-created value. It is a demand that the fruits of labor be protected and the rents of nature be shared. It is a recognition that the earth, in the words of Thomas Paine, is "the common property of the human race," and that those who monopolize its most valuable portions owe a debt to those they exclude.

The intellectual foundations are unassailable—from Locke's proviso to Ricardo's theory of rent to George's synthesis to the modern Henry George Theorem. The empirical evidence is encouraging—from Harrisburg to Hong Kong to Singapore. The moral logic is compelling—reward production, not privilege; tax what you take, not what you make.

We have tried every other tax system. We have taxed income, punishing the productive. We have taxed sales, punishing the consumer. We have taxed buildings, punishing the builder. And through it all, we have left untouched the greatest source of unearned wealth in human history—the rental value of the earth itself.

It is time to complete what Henry George began. It is time to make the earth a common treasury. It is time—for justice, for efficiency, for prosperity—to capture the land.

"We do not want to rob the rich. We simply want to stop robbing the poor." — Attributed to Henry George

A Speech for the Common Heritage: Land Value Taxation

Ladies and gentlemen, fellow citizens,

I stand before you today to speak of an injustice so vast, so deeply woven into our daily lives, that we have forgotten it is an injustice at all. I speak of the private collection of land rent — the wealth that springs not from any man's labor, but from the very presence of community itself.

The Forgotten Question

Two and a half centuries ago, the great economists — Adam Smith, David Ricardo, John Stuart Mill — understood something we have allowed ourselves to forget: that land is fundamentally different from the fruits of human effort. When a farmer tills the soil, when a carpenter shapes wood, when an engineer designs a bridge — that is creation. That belongs to the creator.

But the land itself? The location value of a corner lot in Manhattan? The mineral wealth beneath the prairie? The view of the harbor?

No human being made those things.

And yet, today, we permit the private capture of trillions of dollars in wealth that belongs — by natural right, by the logic of justice — to all of us, collectively, as members of the human family.

Henry George saw this clearly in 1879, when he asked the question that still haunts us: Why, in an age of unprecedented technological progress, does poverty persist? Why do millions struggle for shelter while land values soar beyond their reach? Why does the wealth generated by civilization itself flow upward into the hands of those who merely hold title to the earth?

The answer, my friends, is as simple as it is profound: We tax the wrong things.

What We Tax Today — And Why It Fails

Think of what our current system punishes.

We tax your wages — so you take home less for every hour you work. We tax the profits of businesses — so entrepreneurs think twice before hiring, before building, before creating. We tax sales — so every purchase costs more than it should. We tax buildings — so landlords leave lots vacant rather than develop them, and homeowners hesitate to improve their properties.

In short: We penalize everything we want more of — work, production, exchange, improvement — while we subsidize the one thing that creates no wealth at all: the private holding of valuable land.

Is it any wonder that speculation runs rampant? That housing costs consume ever-larger portions of family income? That productive businesses struggle while landowners grow rich by doing nothing but sitting on property and watching the community create value around them?

The Georgist Vision

Now imagine a different world.

Imagine a nation that funds its entire government — its roads, its schools, its courts, its defense, its parks — through a single tax on the unimproved value of land.

Imagine that when you earn a dollar, you keep that dollar. When you build a home, when you start a business, when you invest in your community — you are rewarded, not penalized.

But imagine that when you hold a valuable piece of land — a privilege that excludes your fellow citizens from that location — you pay the community for that privilege, in proportion to the value the community itself has created there.

This is not confiscation. This is justice.

You built the building? It's yours. You grew the crops? They're yours. You opened the store? The profits are yours. We tax none of it. But the land beneath — the location value that rises because a school was built nearby, because a transit line was extended, because your neighbors invested in their homes and businesses — that value belongs to all of us, and it should fund the services that benefit all of us.

Why It Works

The economics here are not mysterious. They are elegant.

First, a land value tax cannot be passed on to tenants or consumers. Unlike every other tax, it falls on something whose supply is fixed. No one can produce more land; no one can take their land and move it to another country. The tax simply converts private land rent into public revenue — with no distortion of the market.

Second, it eliminates speculation. Today, vast tracts of land sit idle in cities across the nation — held by speculators who wait for values to rise, contributing nothing while the housing crisis deepens. A full land value tax makes hoarding unprofitable. Land must be used productively, or it must be released to someone who will use it. Imagine the effect on housing supply alone.

Third, it returns wealth to the community that created it. When a city builds a subway line, property values along the route skyrocket. Today, that windfall enriches private landowners. Under a Georgist system, that value flows back to fund the public services that generated it in the first place. It is a self-reinforcing cycle of prosperity.

Fourth, it requires no complex bureaucracy. One tax. One base. One assessment. No loopholes, no offshore shelters, no armies of accountants gaming the system. Land cannot be hidden. Its value, being created by the community, is known to the community.

Answering the Objections

Some will say: "But people have invested in land! You'll destroy their savings!"

I say: people have invested in land because we have allowed them to privatize community-created value. The transition must be gradual and just — perhaps beginning with offsetting reductions in income and sales taxes — but the moral case does not change. No one has a natural right to unearned wealth at the expense of their neighbors.

Some will say: "But the government is inefficient. Why give it more money?"

I say: a land value tax is not about the size of government. It is about the source of revenue. You want smaller government? Fine — but let us fund even that smaller government justly, without punishing labor and enterprise.

Some will say: "This has never been tried."

I say: look at Singapore, where land value capture funds much of public revenue and housing is more accessible than in any comparable city. Look at Denmark, at Estonia, at parts of Australia and New Zealand. Wherever even partial land value taxation has been implemented, the results have been prosperity, reduced speculation, and more equitable growth.

The Moral Heart of the Matter

But I confess, my friends, that for me this is not primarily an economic argument. It is a moral one.

Every child born into this world has an equal right to the earth — the common inheritance of all humanity. When we allow some to monopolize that inheritance and charge others for access to it, we create a system in which the many must labor to enrich the few, not for anything the few have created, but merely for permission to exist on the surface of the planet.

This is not freedom. This is not justice. This is a feudal arrangement dressed in the language of modernity.

And we can do better.

We can build a society in which labor is untaxed, enterprise is encouraged, and the wealth that flows from our shared presence in community is used to benefit all members of that community.

A Call to Action

So I call upon you — citizens, policymakers, economists, thinkers, dreamers — to take this vision seriously. Read Henry George. Study the mathematics. Examine the evidence. And then ask yourselves:

What kind of society do we want to be?

One that taxes work and rewards idleness? One that penalizes productivity and protects speculation?

Or one that recognizes the earth as our common heritage, frees labor and enterprise from the burden of taxation, and ensures that the bounty of civilization flows back to the people who create it?

The choice is ours. The time is now. And the principle is as old as justice itself:

The earth belongs to all of us — equally, inalienably, forever.

Let us build a tax system worthy of that truth.

Thank you.

The Ground Beneath Our Feet: A Case for the Land Value Tax as the Sole Source of Public Revenue

For centuries, philosophers and economists have grappled with the question of how to build a just and prosperous society. It is the proposal to replace all current taxes with a single levy: a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land. The core of the argument rests on a critical distinction between what individuals rightfully create and what nature provides for all. When a person builds a factory, invents a new technology, or provides a valuable service, they have created new wealth. Taxing these productive activities—whether through income, sales, or corporate taxes—acts as a penalty on productivity, discouraging work, innovation, and investment. Land, however, is fundamentally different. Its value is not created by the landowner’s labor or ingenuity. Rather, a plot of land accrues value from the community that surrounds it: the construction of public roads and transit, the quality of local schools, the safety provided by police and fire services, and the economic activity generated by neighbors. This increase in value, known as economic rent, is an unearned increment bestowed upon the landholder by society. It is therefore not only fair but just that this community-created value be recaptured for public benefit. A 100% Land Value Tax (LVT) on the unimproved value does precisely this, ensuring that the value we all create is used for us all, without confiscating a single dollar of individually earned income.

Beyond its compelling fairness, the economic efficiency of a full LVT is unparalleled. Our current tax system is a labyrinth of disincentives. Income taxes reduce the reward for working overtime or acquiring new skills. Sales taxes make goods more expensive, suppressing consumption. To avoid losing money, they are compelled to put the land to its best and highest use—building housing, opening a business, or selling to someone who will. Skeptics often raise concerns, but these are based on misconceptions. Some argue that taxing land at 100% of its rental value is a form of confiscation. It makes the revitalization of downtown cores more profitable than paving over farmland on the urban fringe.

In conclusion, the implementation of a 100% land value tax on the unimproved value of land is more than a fiscal policy; it is a commitment to a more equitable and dynamic society. It is the most efficient tax conceivable, one that cannot stifle production but instead galvanizes it, turning idle speculation into productive enterprise. By fully capturing land rent for the public treasury, we can liberate human enterprise from the drag of punitive taxes, foster sustainable development, and create a world where everyone shares in the value of our common inheritance. Core Principle: The Distinction Between Land and Capital

The entire philosophy rests on a critical distinction between three factors of production:

  1. Land: All natural resources, geographical locations, and natural opportunities. This includes the physical land itself, mineral deposits, water rights, the radio spectrum, etc. The key characteristic is that land is not created by human labor; its supply is fixed.
  2. Labor: Human effort applied to production.
  3. Capital: Wealth (like tools, buildings, machinery) created by labor for the purpose of producing more goods.

Georgists argue that because the supply of land is fixed, its value is not created by the individual landowner. Instead, land value is created by the community. A plot of land in a desert is worthless. The same plot in a thriving city is incredibly valuable because of the public infrastructure (roads, schools, police), economic activity, and population surrounding it.

The "Single Tax" Proposal: A 100% Tax on Land Value (LVT)

The proposal is to levy a tax equal to the full annual rental value of a piece of land, ignoring any improvements made on it. This is often called a Land Value Tax (LVT) or the "Single Tax."

  • What is taxed: The value of the location itself. If you own an empty lot in a city, you are taxed based on what someone would pay to rent that lot for a year.
  • What is NOT taxed: Any building, crop, or structure on the land—the "improvements." Your wages, profits from a business, sales of goods, and investments in capital are also untaxed.

Supposed Benefits and Reasons for Adoption

1. Economic Efficiency and Elimination of Deadweight Loss

  • Reason: Most taxes (on income, sales, or business profits) discourage the very activity you are taxing. Taxing income can discourage work; taxing sales can discourage consumption; taxing capital discourages investment. This is known as a "deadweight loss" to the economy.
  • Benefit: Because the supply of land is fixed, a tax on its value cannot discourage its production. You cannot hide land or decide to produce less of it. Therefore, an LVT is considered an economically efficient tax that does not distort market incentives. It actually encourages productive use of land because holding it idle becomes expensive.

2. The Ethical Argument: Ending Unearned Wealth (Economic Rent)

  • Reason: The increase in land value due to community efforts is an "unearned increment" or economic rent. Georgists view this as the most fundamental form of economic injustice. A landowner can become wealthy simply by owning a strategically located piece of land and doing nothing, while a worker's wages are taxed.
  • Benefit: The LVT recaptures this community-created value for the community. It ensures that the wealth generated by societal progress benefits everyone, not just a few landowners. It is seen as a way to socialize economic rent while privatizing the rewards of labor and capital.

3. Progressive Wealth Distribution and Poverty Reduction

  • Reason: Land ownership is heavily concentrated. A tax that falls primarily on landowners—who tend to be wealthier—is inherently progressive. By removing other regressive taxes (like sales taxes), the overall tax burden shifts from the poor and middle class to those holding valuable, often underutilized, land.
  • Benefit: This could significantly reduce inequality. The public revenue generated could be used to fund public services or even distributed as a universal basic income (a concept often called the "citizen's dividend"), ensuring everyone shares in the value created by their collective society.

4. Optimal Land Use and Curbing Speculation

  • Reason: Under the current system, it can be profitable to hold land vacant, waiting for its value to rise (land speculation). This leads to urban sprawl, housing shortages in valuable areas, and inefficient use of resources.
  • Benefit: The LVT makes it costly to hold land idle. It creates a powerful incentive for landowners to develop their property to its "highest and best use" to generate income to pay the tax. This would theoretically lead to more dense, efficient, and affordable urban development, reducing housing costs and combating sprawl.

5. Simplicity and Reduction of Corruption

  • Reason: A complex tax code with income, corporate, sales, and property taxes is difficult and expensive to administer and can be gamed through loopholes.
  • Benefit: As a "Single Tax," the LVT would be far simpler to administer. Land cannot be hidden or moved offshore. Its value is relatively easy to assess compared to income or complex corporate profits. This transparency would reduce administrative costs and opportunities for tax evasion and corruption.

Summary of the Rationale

In the clearest terms, the Georgist argument is:

Public revenue should be raised by taxing what we all create together (land value), instead of taxing what we create as individuals (our labor and capital). This would lead to a more efficient, equitable, and prosperous economy by rewarding productivity, discouraging speculative hoarding, and ensuring the community benefits from the value it generates.

Important Caveats and Context

  • "100% Tax" is a Theoretical Goal: In practice, no modern Georgist policy proposes an immediate, overnight 100% tax. The goal is to gradually shift the tax burden toward land and away from other forms of taxation.
  • Implementation Challenges: Accurate assessment of only the land value, separate from improvements, is a technical challenge, though most assessors' offices already do this to some degree.
  • Political Feasibility: The proposal faces significant political opposition from those with large landholdings who benefit from the current system.

This explanation outlines the ideal outcomes as theorized within the Georgist framework. The actual effects of such a radical shift in tax policy are a subject of ongoing economic debate.

I. Justice: Correcting an Inheritance of Privilege and Restoring Common Rights

At the heart of the Georgist proposal is a timeless truth: land is not a human creation. Its value arises not from the efforts or investments of individual owners, but from natural features and above all from societal factors—population growth, infrastructure, public services, and the bustling activity of communities. When private individuals collect land rent, they are capturing unearned windfalls, passively extracting wealth that rightfully belongs to everyone. As Henry George argued, “The land belongs equally to all.”

A 100% LVT is the fairest tax because:

  • It respects labor and enterprise. Taxing land does not punish productive effort. It stops the unjust enrichment of landowners solely due to community progress.
  • It recognizes the public’s role. Roads, transit, schools, and the very existence of cities make land valuable. The rent flows from public activity and investment, thus it is only fair that it be returned to the public purse.
  • It redresses inequality. Access to valuable land is a birthright, not a reward for skill or work. Capturing its value for all ensures the fortunes of geography and inheritance do not become entrenched sources of poverty and exclusion.

II. Efficiency: The Land Value Tax as the World’s Most Economically Sound Revenue Source

Conventional taxes—on income, sales, capital, or buildings—distort incentives, discourage enterprise, and shrink economies. But a tax on the unimproved value of land is unique: it is economically efficient, and non-distortionary.

  • No deadweight loss. Land is fixed; taxing it does not reduce the supply or discourage its use. Unlike taxes on productive activity, it does not create economic drag (“deadweight loss”).
  • Elimination of speculation and sprawl. When landowners cannot profit merely by waiting for land values to appreciate, they are compelled to put sites to productive use. This reduces speculation, makes housing more affordable, and encourages vibrant, dense cities instead of inefficient sprawl.

  • Universal benefit. The funds gathered from LVT can finance public services everyone uses: education, healthcare, infrastructure, and social programs.

The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax: A Georgist Path to Economic Justice and Efficiency

Introduction

For centuries, economists, philosophers, and policymakers have debated the most just and efficient way to fund public goods while fostering economic prosperity. Among the most compelling solutions is the Land Value Tax (LVT), a policy rooted in the economic philosophy of Henry George, the 19th-century American economist whose seminal work, Progress and Poverty (1879), argued that land rent—the unearned income derived from the mere ownership of land—should be the sole source of government revenue. A 100% LVT on the unimproved value of land would eliminate all other taxes (income, sales, corporate, property improvements) and instead capture the full economic rent generated by land, redistributing it for public benefit.

This essay argues that a 100% LVT is the fairest, most efficient, and most economically sound tax system possible. It would eliminate speculative land bubbles, reduce inequality, spur productive investment, and fund public goods without distorting economic behavior. By shifting the tax burden entirely onto land rent, society can unlock vast untapped wealth, end artificial scarcity, and create a more dynamic and equitable economy.

I. The Moral Case: Land Rent is Unearned and Should Belong to Society

1. Land is a Common Inheritance, Not a Private Creation

Unlike capital or labor, land is not produced by human effort—it is a gift of nature, a finite resource that no individual or corporation created. The value of land arises not from the owner’s labor but from society’s collective efforts—population growth, infrastructure development, public services, and economic activity. When a landowner benefits from rising land values due to a new subway line, school, or business district, they are capturing wealth created by the community, not themselves.

As Henry George argued: > "The equal right of all men to the use of land is as clear as their equal right to breathe the air—it is a right proclaimed by the fact of their existence."

A 100% LVT simply returns this socially created value to its rightful owners: the public.

2. Land Speculation is Parasitic and Exploitative

Under the current system, landowners profit not by improving land but by hoarding it, waiting for its value to rise, and extracting rent from those who need it. This artificial scarcity drives up housing costs, stifles development, and forces workers to pay exorbitant rents to absentee landlords.

A 100% LVT would eliminate speculative landholding by making it unprofitable to sit on idle land. If landowners must pay the full annual rental value of their land to the government, they will either:

  • Develop it productively (building homes, businesses, or farms), or
  • Sell it to someone who will.

This would dramatically increase the housing supply, lowering costs and making homeownership more accessible.

3. Current Taxes Punish Productivity; LVT Rewards It

Today’s tax system is backward and unjust:

  • Income taxes penalize work and innovation.
  • Sales taxes disproportionately harm the poor.
  • Corporate taxes discourage investment and job creation.
  • Property taxes on improvements discourage homeowners from renovating or expanding.

A 100% LVT, by contrast, does not tax labor, capital, or improvements—only the unimproved value of land. This means:

  • Workers keep 100% of their wages (no income tax).
  • Businesses pay no taxes on profits or investments (no corporate tax).
  • Homeowners are not penalized for improving their property (no tax on buildings, only land).

This shifts the tax burden from productive activity to unearned wealth, aligning incentives with economic growth and fairness.

II. The Economic Case: Efficiency, Growth, and Stability

1. LVT Eliminates Deadweight Loss and Boosts Productivity

Most taxes distort economic behavior, creating deadweight loss—the inefficiency that arises when people change their actions to avoid taxes. For example:

  • Income taxes discourage work and entrepreneurship.
  • Sales taxes reduce consumption, harming businesses.
  • Corporate taxes lead to tax avoidance and capital flight.

A 100% LVT, however, cannot be avoided or passed on—land is immobile, and its value is determined by location and demand, not by the owner’s actions. Since landowners cannot reduce the supply of land (unlike labor or capital), they cannot shift the tax burden onto others.

This makes LVT the most efficient tax possible, as it does not discourage productive activity—instead, it encourages optimal land use.

2. LVT Prevents Land Bubbles and Financial Crises

One of the root causes of economic instability is land speculation, which leads to boom-and-bust cycles. When land prices rise artificially, banks issue mortgages based on inflated values, leading to housing bubbles (as seen in 2008). When the bubble bursts, millions lose their homes, and the economy crashes.

A 100% LVT would prevent speculative bubbles by:

  • Making land hoarding unprofitable (owners must pay the full rental value, so they either develop land or sell it).
  • Stabilizing land prices (since land is no longer a speculative asset, its value reflects actual use, not future expectations).
  • Reducing debt-fueled speculation (banks would lend based on productive capacity, not land value).

3. LVT Funds Public Goods Without Distortion

Under the current system, governments struggle to fund essential services because:

  • Taxes on labor and capital reduce economic activity, shrinking the tax base.
  • Wealthy landowners and corporations avoid taxes through loopholes.
  • Public goods (roads, schools, healthcare) are underfunded, leading to decaying infrastructure and inequality.

A 100% LVT solves this by:

  • Capturing the full economic rent of land, which grows with population and prosperity (unlike income or sales taxes, which shrink in recessions).
  • Eliminating tax evasion (land cannot be hidden offshore).
  • Providing a stable, growing revenue stream for public services.

4. LVT Encourages Urban Density and Reduces Sprawl

Today, suburban sprawl is encouraged by low property taxes on undeveloped land, leading to:

  • Wasted land (parking lots, vacant lots, underused space).
  • Long commutes, increasing pollution and infrastructure costs.
  • Higher housing costs (artificial scarcity in cities).

A 100% LVT would reverse this by:

  • Penalizing land hoarding, forcing owners to develop land efficiently.
  • Encouraging high-density, mixed-use development (since landowners maximize value by building upward, not outward).
  • Reducing urban sprawl, lowering infrastructure costs and environmental damage.

III. The Practical Case: How a 100% LVT Would Work

1. Implementation: Phasing Out Other Taxes

Transitioning to a 100% LVT would require a gradual phase-out of other taxes to avoid economic disruption. A possible approach:

  1. Start with a modest LVT (e.g., 1-2% of land value) while reducing income and sales taxes.
  2. Increase the LVT rate over 10-20 years while eliminating other taxes.
  3. Eventually reach 100% LVT, with no other taxes in place.

This prevents sudden shocks while allowing businesses and individuals to adjust.

2. Valuation and Administration

  • Land value is assessed annually based on market data, zoning, and location (not improvements).
  • Owners pay the full rental value (what they would earn if they rented the land).
  • No exemptions—every landowner pays, including governments, churches, and corporations.

3. Compensation for Current Landowners?

Some argue that suddenly imposing a 100% LVT would be unfair to current landowners. However:

  • Land values are already socially created—owners did not "earn" the increase in value from population growth or public investment.
  • A gradual phase-in (as described above) allows landowners to adjust.
  • Those who bought land at high prices (e.g., in cities) would see lower net costs because other taxes (income, sales, corporate) would disappear.

4. Global Precedents: LVT Works in Practice

Several places have successfully implemented LVT, proving its feasibility:

  • Pennsylvania (USA): Cities like Pittsburgh and Harrisburg used LVT to revitalize downtowns and reduce blight.
  • Denmark: A land tax helped stabilize housing markets and reduce speculation.
  • Singapore: A high land tax (though not 100%) has kept housing affordable despite rapid growth.
  • Estonia: A land value tax has encouraged efficient land use and reduced sprawl.

These examples show that LVT works in the real world, not just in theory.

IV. Counterarguments and Rebuttals

1. "A 100% LVT is Too Radical—People Won’t Accept It"

Rebuttal:

  • Most people don’t own land—they rent or have mortgages. A 100% LVT would lower rents and housing costs, benefiting the majority.
  • Homeowners would pay less (since they’d no longer pay income, sales, or property taxes on improvements).
  • Businesses would thrive (no corporate taxes, no payroll taxes, no sales taxes).
  • The only losers would be land speculators and absentee landlords—who are extracting wealth without contributing to society.

2. "Landowners Would Be Forced to Sell"

Rebuttal:

  • Only if they cannot afford the tax—which means they were not using the land productively.
  • Those who develop land (farmers, homeowners, businesses) would pay less in total taxes (since income, sales, and corporate taxes disappear).
  • The tax is on the land’s rental value, not the owner’s income—so if the land is valuable, the owner can rent it out or develop it to cover the tax.

3. "Government Would Have Too Much Power Over Land"

Rebuttal:

  • Government already controls land use through zoning laws—LVT simply aligns incentives with efficient use.
  • A 100% LVT does not mean government owns the land—it just captures the rent, leaving ownership and use in private hands.
  • Unlike eminent domain, LVT does not seize land—it merely taxes the unearned increment of value.

4. "It’s Unfair to Tax Land That Was Bought at High Prices"

Rebuttal:

  • Land values are not "earned"—they are created by society. If a landowner paid a high price, it was because someone else (the previous owner) captured the socially created value.
  • Under LVT, land prices would stabilize—no more speculative bubbles, so future buyers would not overpay.
  • The elimination of other taxes would offset the LVT for most people.

V. Conclusion: A 100% LVT is the Key to a Just and Prosperous Society

Henry George’s vision of a single tax on land value is not just an economic theory—it is a moral imperative and a practical solution to many of society’s deepest problems. A 100% LVT would:

✅ End land speculation and housing bubbles, making homeownership affordable. ✅ Eliminate poverty and inequality by ensuring that wealth created by society returns to society. ✅ Boost economic growth by removing taxes on labor, capital, and innovation. ✅ Fund public goods efficiently without distorting behavior. ✅ Encourage sustainable urban development by penalizing sprawl and land hoarding. ✅ Create a fairer, more dynamic economy where people are rewarded for productivity, not luck of birth.

The alternative—continuing to tax labor and capital while allowing landowners to extract unearned wealth—is unjust, inefficient, and unsustainable. The time has come to implement a 100% Land Value Tax and build a society where prosperity is shared, not monopolized.

As Henry George wrote: > "The equal right of all men to the use of land is as clear as their equal right to breathe the air—it is a right proclaimed by the fact of their existence. For we cannot suppose that some men have a right to be in this world and others no right."

It is time to act on this truth and reclaim the common inheritance of land for the benefit of all.

7. Historical & Theoretical Support

Georgism is not a fringe idea—it has been endorsed by many prominent economists and thinkers, including:

  • Adam Smith (The Wealth of Nations): "Ground rents are a still more proper subject of taxation than the rent of houses."
  • John Stuart Mill: Advocated for taxing the "unearned increment" of land value.

Georgism argues that a single tax on unimproved land value would: ✅ Eliminate economic distortions (no deadweight loss). ✅ End land speculation (encouraging productive use). ✅ Tax unearned wealth (fairer than taxing labor or capital). ✅ Simplify taxation (no need for income, sales, or corporate taxes). ✅ Boost wages & employment (by reducing land costs). ✅ Protect the environment (by discouraging sprawl). ✅ Be administratively simple (land cannot be hidden).

Model Response:

The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax: Why capturing the full rental value of land for public benefit is the most just, efficient, and economically transformative policy available to modern society

Introduction: A Revolution in Political Economy That Never Fully Arrived

In 1879, Henry George published Progress and Poverty, one of the most influential works of economic and political philosophy in human history. Its central insight—that the economic rent of land, arising not from the labor or investment of any individual but from the collective activity and growth of the community, rightfully belongs to the community as a whole—offered a solution to the paradox of increasing poverty amid rising wealth that continues to resonate with devastating clarity in the twenty-first century. George proposed a "single tax": the complete capture of land rent through a tax assessed at 100% of the unimproved value of land, with all other taxes abolished. This policy, known today as the Land Value Tax (LVT), is not merely an interesting fiscal instrument. It is, I will argue, the single most just, efficient, and economically beneficial revenue mechanism ever conceived—a mechanism that, if fully implemented, would eliminate the worst distortions of capitalism, dramatically reduce inequality, unleash economic productivity, and render obsolete the panoply of destructive taxes that currently strangle enterprise, consumption, and human freedom.

The thesis of this essay is straightforward: every dollar of land rent belongs to the community. A 100% LVT is not a radical confiscation of property; it is the rightful return of common wealth to its rightful owners—the people. This essay will demonstrate, in comprehensive detail, why the full capture of land rent is fair, why it is uniquely efficient, and why it should serve as the sole source of government revenue, replacing all income taxes, sales taxes, property taxes on improvements, capital gains taxes, and the rest of the bureaucratic fiscal apparatus that distorts markets and impoverishes citizens.

Part I: The Moral and Philosophical Foundation — Land as a Common Inheritance

1.1 The Fundamental Distinction: Land vs. Capital

At the heart of Georgist economics lies a distinction that most economic traditions have blurred or ignored entirely: the distinction between land and capital. In common parlance, "property" is treated as a monolithic category, but George, following the classical economists—Adam Smith, David Ricardo, John Stuart Mill, and others—recognized that land and capital are fundamentally different in their economic nature, their moral status, and their relationship to human labor.

Land is the earth itself: the ground, the minerals beneath it, the water on and under it, the electromagnetic spectrum, the geostationary orbits, the airspace, and all natural resources that existed before any human being set foot upon it. Land is not produced by anyone. It is not the result of effort, ingenuity, or investment. It is a gift of nature, a common inheritance that belongs, in the deepest moral sense, to all of humanity equally.

Capital, by contrast, is the product of human labor and saving. It includes buildings, machinery, tools, infrastructure, inventions, and all improvements made to land. Capital is created by individuals and groups who expend effort, take risks, and invest their time and resources. Capital rightfully belongs to those who create it.

The Georgist argument is not a call for the expropriation of capital. It is not an argument against private ownership of improvements. It is, rather, an argument that the rent of land—the income derived from ownership of land itself, apart from any improvements—belongs to the community as a whole, because the community as a whole is the ultimate source of that rent.

1.2 The Community as the Source of Land Value

Why does land have value? This question, which may seem elementary, is the crux of the entire Georgist argument. Consider two parcels of land: one in the middle of a vast, unpopulated desert, and one in the center of a thriving metropolis. The desert land may be worth almost nothing, while the urban land may be worth millions of dollars per acre. Yet the physical characteristics of the land—its soil, its topography, its climate—may be virtually identical. The difference in value is not due to anything the landowner did; it is due to the activity of the community: the roads, schools, hospitals, businesses, and populations that surround the land and make it valuable.

This is the Georgist insight: land value is a social product. It is created not by the landowner but by the community. When a city builds a subway station, nearby land values rise—not because the landowner did anything, but because the community invested in public infrastructure. When a new school is built, when a neighborhood becomes fashionable, when a city attracts industry—land values rise, and the landowner profits from the collective effort of others.

This principle has profound moral implications. If land value is created by the community, then the community, through its government, has a right to capture that value for public purposes. The landowner's claim to the full rental value of the land is, in the deepest sense, a claim to the product of other people's labor—a claim that is morally indistinguishable from theft.

1.3 John Stuart Mill and the Unearned Increment

John Stuart Mill, one of the most influential economists and philosophers of the nineteenth century, recognized this principle clearly. He wrote:

> "Landlords grow richer in their sleep without working, risking, or economizing. What they have merely to do is to sit still and allow land values to increase through the efforts of the community."

Mill called the increase in land value the "unearned increment" and argued that it rightfully belonged to the community. But Mill, for all his brilliance, only went so far as to propose a partial tax on the unearned increment. George went further: he argued that all land rent—both the incremental increase and the baseline value—belonged to the community, and that a tax capturing 100% of land rent would be sufficient to fund all government operations, rendering all other taxes unnecessary.

1.4 The Landowner as an Unproductive Parasite

This is the most controversial aspect of the Georgist argument, and it deserves careful treatment. George did not argue that landowners are morally deficient as human beings. He recognized that most landowners are ordinary people who purchased land in good faith. But the institution of private land ownership, as it exists under current law, creates a class of individuals who derive income not from labor or investment but from the mere act of holding title to land. This income is, by definition, unearned. It is a rent—a payment for the privilege of excluding others from the use of a common resource.

In a Georgist system, this would not be a moral failing on the part of the individual landowner. It would simply be the recognition that land, as a common inheritance, should be managed for the benefit of all. The 100% LVT does not prohibit private ownership of land; it simply ensures that the economic benefit of ownership accrues to the community, not to the individual. The landowner retains full use and control of the land; what changes is that the landowner must pay the community the full rental value of the land each year, rather than keeping that value as a private windfall.

Part II: The Case for Fairness — Why Land Rent Belongs to the People

2.1 Justice in the Distribution of Wealth

The question of fairness is not merely academic; it is the foundation of social stability and democratic governance. A society in which a small class of individuals can extract enormous wealth from the mere ownership of land, while the vast majority of people must work for wages, pay taxes on their labor, and struggle to afford housing, is a society in deep injustice.

Consider the following facts about the current distribution of land wealth:

  • In the United States, the total value of all land is estimated at over $30 trillion—far exceeding the total value of all improvements on that land. This means that a substantial portion of the nation's wealth is concentrated in the ownership of land, a resource that was not produced by anyone.
  • In major cities like London, New York, and Tokyo, land values account for a majority of total property value. A single parcel of land in Manhattan can be worth more than an entire town in a rural area, not because of anything the landowner did, but because of the collective activity of millions of people who live and work in the city.
  • The wealth of the wealthiest individuals in the world is largely derived from the ownership of land and natural resources. Elon Musk's wealth, Jeff Bezos's wealth, and the wealth of countless other billionaires is built, in large part, on the foundation of land ownership.

This is not a coincidence. It is the predictable result of a system that allows private individuals to capture the full value of a common resource. The Georgist argument is not that landowners are greedy or immoral; it is that the system of private land ownership, as it currently exists, is inherently unfair. The 100% LVT corrects this unfairness by returning land rent to its rightful owner: the community.

2.2 The Principle of Equal Rights

The Georgist argument for fairness rests on a fundamental principle: every person has an equal right to the earth. This principle is enshrined in no constitution, but it is a basic moral truth. The earth is the common inheritance of all humanity; no individual has a natural right to exclude others from its use. Private land ownership is a social convention, a practical arrangement that allows for the efficient use of land, but it does not confer a moral right to the exclusive benefit of a natural resource.

The 100% LVT is the most practical way to implement this principle. It does not abolish private ownership; it simply ensures that the economic benefit of ownership is shared equally. Every citizen receives, in the form of public services and reduced taxes, the full rental value of the land. No citizen is excluded from the benefits of land ownership; all citizens are equal beneficiaries.

2.3 The Fairness of Replacing Other Taxes

One of the most powerful arguments for the 100% LVT is that it would replace the entire current tax system—income taxes, sales taxes, property taxes on improvements, payroll taxes, capital gains taxes, estate taxes, and all the rest. These taxes are not only inefficient; they are deeply unfair.

Income taxes penalize productive effort. The more you work, the more you pay. This is the opposite of what a just tax system should do. A just tax system should encourage productive effort and penalize unproductive hoarding. The LVT does exactly this.

Sales taxes are regressive, hitting the poor hardest. A person who spends all their income on necessities pays a higher percentage in sales taxes than a billionaire who saves most of his income. The LVT is progressive, hitting the wealthiest landowners hardest, because they hold the most valuable land.

Property taxes on improvements discourage construction and investment. Every time a landowner builds a new building, they increase their tax bill. This is perverse: we should be encouraging construction and investment, not penalizing it. The LVT, by taxing only the unimproved value of land and not improvements, encourages construction and investment to the maximum extent possible.

Payroll taxes discourage employment. Every time a business hires a worker, it must pay payroll taxes. This makes employment more expensive and reduces the number of jobs available. The LVT does not discourage employment because it does not tax labor or investment.

Capital gains taxes discourage investment. Every time an investor realizes a gain, they must pay taxes. This discourages risk-taking and entrepreneurship. The LVT does not tax capital gains because it does not tax capital; it taxes only land.

2.4 Addressing the "But I Bought My Land" Objection

A common objection to the LVT is that it is unfair to current landowners who purchased their land in good faith, expecting to keep the full rental value. This objection has some intuitive force, but it is ultimately unpersuasive for several reasons.

First, the concept of private land ownership is itself a social convention, not a natural right. The government already taxes land (through property taxes, capital gains taxes, and other mechanisms), and the government already imposes regulations on land use (zoning, environmental regulations, etc.). The LVT is not a departure from the existing system; it is a refinement of it.

Second, the LVT is not a confiscation of capital. It does not seize land; it seizes the annual rental value of land. The landowner retains full ownership and control of the land. What changes is that the landowner must pay the community for the privilege of holding title to the land. This is analogous to a lease: the landowner pays an annual fee for the right to use the land, and that fee goes to the community.

Third, the LVT would be implemented gradually, not abruptly. A gradual phase-in would allow landowners to adjust their plans and investments. Standard public finance theory teaches the "deadweight loss" triangle: all taxes on production and exchange distort behavior, shrink the economic pie, and create inefficiency. Modern government spending in developed nations typically hovers between 30% and 45% of GDP. Abolishing those "deadweight" taxes would cause a massive capitalization effect, exploding land values (and thus the LVT base) as the economy is unshackled. A 100% LVT, by eliminating the tax burden on labor and capital, unlocks a torrent of productive energy that flows directly into the land rent base.   4. Privacy: The state has no need to know your income, your spending habits, your investments, or your family structure. Your economic life is once again your own.

This is taxation consistent with a free society: transparent, unavoidable only by selling the asset (which transfers the obligation to a more efficient user), and blind to the private affairs of the citizen.
